content_blocks.title: Why this matters
content_blocks.text: Data transformations should be explicit and auditable: define the rule, check row counts and keys, and preserve the reason for each cleaning choice. The example is intentionally small so you can predict its result before checking it in a local R session.

content_blocks.title: Work through it
content_blocks.text: Compare before/after row counts, check a key or range invariant, and record how missing or duplicate records were handled. Change one input or condition at a time, compare the observed result with your prediction, and write down one limitation.

content_blocks.title: R example: Duplicates, Inconsistencies, and Outliers
content_blocks.code:
# Lesson 113: Duplicates, Inconsistencies, and Outliers
example_rows <- data.frame(group = c("A", "B", "A"), amount = c(3, 4, 5))
aggregate(amount ~ group, data = example_rows, sum)

content_blocks.title: Common pitfall
content_blocks.text: Do not treat a syntactically plausible example as proof of correctness. For duplicates, inconsistencies, and outliers, check the input type, missing/empty cases, output shape, and domain assumptions.

common_mistakes.problem: Removing rows before measuring how much information is missing.
common_mistakes.why: Missingness or outliers may be systematic and can bias the result.
common_mistakes.fix: Count affected rows, state the rule, compare before/after summaries and keep an audit trail.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating every repeated key as an accidental duplicate.
common_mistakes.why: Repeated rows may represent repeated events or valid measurements.
common_mistakes.fix: Define the expected key grain and review examples before deleting records.

common_mistakes.problem: Changing categories or units without documenting the transformation.
common_mistakes.why: Silent standardization makes results difficult to reproduce.
common_mistakes.fix: Record the mapping rule and add a validation check.
